title: Green on the fifth try
scenario: A team wired its support-agent evals into GitHub Actions last month. Developers now complain that the gate blocks merges at random, yet a prompt change still broke old behavior last week. You review the workflow and the run history (exhibit).
exhibit:
(made-up example data)

WORKFLOW: support-agent evals
  trigger:      pull_request
  runs:         full suite, 900 tasks, model graders, 1 trial per task
  timeout:      none
  api key:      written in the workflow file as a plain value
  gate:         pass if overall score >= 85%
  environment:  all trials share one scratch folder, never cleaned

LAST 5 RUNS ON main (no code change between them)
  overall score: 88%, 84%, 87%, 83%, 89%
  runs that blocked: 2 of 5; developers re-run until green

PR #412 (prompt change)
  overall score: 86%  -> gate passes
  regression suite (120 tasks): 3 tasks that passed for months now fail

questions.prompt: The score swings between 83% and 89% with no code change. What is the best fix?

options.text: Lower the gate to 80%, so noise can no longer block a merge.
options.explanation: A lower bar hides real drops too. The noise would still be there, and so would the mystery.

options.text: Run several trials per task and compare with a stored baseline.
options.explanation: Right. Outputs vary, so one trial per task is noisy. Anthropic runs multiple trials because a task that passed on one run might fail on the next. A stored baseline shows whether a change is real.

options.text: Keep re-running a blocked build until it turns green.
options.explanation: That is what the team does now. It means a real failure can also pass on a lucky run.

options.text: Replace every model grader with exact string matching.
options.explanation: Exact match lacks nuance for open answers. Model graders add some noise too, but the main cause here is one trial per task.

questions.prompt: PR #412 scores 86% and passes the gate, but 3 old tasks now fail. What is wrong with the gate?

options.text: It should block on the regression suite, which must stay near 100%.
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic says regression evals should have a nearly 100% pass rate. An overall average can hide broken tasks.

options.text: Nothing. The overall score is above the bar, so the PR can merge.
options.explanation: The average mixes new and old tasks. Three tasks that passed for months are now broken, which is the case a gate exists to stop.

options.text: It should wait for a human to read every transcript in the suite.
options.explanation: Reading transcripts is useful, but it does not replace an automatic gate on every pull request.

options.text: It should drop the 3 tasks, since they started failing only now.
options.explanation: Dropping failing tasks hides regressions. They failed because the change broke them.

questions.prompt: The API key is written in the workflow file as plain text. What do the Claude Code docs say?

options.text: It is fine if the repository is private and few people have access.
options.explanation: The docs say never to commit keys to the repository, whoever can see it.

options.text: Move the key into the eval task files, which are read-only.
options.explanation: Task files live in the repository too, so the key would still be committed.

options.text: Store it as a GitHub secret and give the workflow only needed permissions.
options.explanation: Right. The docs say to store keys as secrets and reference them in the workflow, and to grant only the permissions needed.

options.text: Encrypt the key in the workflow file and decrypt it in a step.
options.explanation: The encrypted key and its decryption secret still end up in the repository. Store it as a GitHub secret.

questions.prompt: The full 900-task suite runs on every pull request, with no timeout. What fits best?

options.text: Run the full suite only after merging, so pull requests stay fast.
options.explanation: Then regressions reach the main branch first. The point of CI is to stop a change before it ships.

options.text: Remove the grader calls on pull requests to save run time.
options.explanation: Without graders there is nothing to gate on. Choose a smaller suite, not no scoring.

options.text: Add parallel runners without limit, so everything finishes quickly.
options.explanation: Each run costs minutes and tokens. The docs advise limiting parallel runs.

options.text: Run a fast regression suite on PRs and the full suite on a schedule.
options.explanation: Right. This is the split from the lesson (our plan). The Claude Code docs advise workflow timeouts and concurrency limits to stop runaway cost.

questions.prompt: All trials share one scratch folder that is never cleaned. What does Anthropic advise?

options.text: Start every trial from a clean environment.
options.explanation: Right. Shared state, such as leftover files, can cause correlated failures or inflate scores. Anthropic saw Claude read git history from earlier trials.

options.text: Keep the shared folder, since the same files make results comparable.
options.explanation: Anthropic warns that shared state can inflate performance as well as cause failures.

options.text: Clean the folder only after a trial fails, to save time on passes.
options.explanation: A pass can be inflated by shared state too, so clean-up cannot depend on the result.

options.text: Give each task its own folder but never clear it between runs.
options.explanation: Files left from earlier runs of the same task can still change the next result.
